warningSignals.description: Top 5 customers represent ~55% of revenue; DoD budget uncertainty creates lumpy backlog conversion
Cybersecurity and cloud engineering talent churn in competitive DC-metro market; wage inflation in cleared-personnel pool

opportunitySignals.description: CMMC 2.0 compliance, cloud migration (JEDI successor), and AI/ML integration across defense agencies create multi-year TAM expansion
Smaller niche-defense IT shops (SAIC, Booz Allen peers) trading at elevated multiples; ManTech's scale and cleared-workforce base position for bolt-on acquisitions

domainRelevance: ManTech is a pure-play defense and intelligence IT services provider, deriving ~75% of revenue from U.S. federal contracts (DoD, intelligence community, civilian agencies). The company specializes in cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure, systems integration, and mission-critical software for classified and unclassified environments. Its cleared-workforce base and CMMC/FedRAMP certifications position it as a critical node in the federal digital-transformation supply chain.
portalRelevance: ManTech serves as a leading indicator of federal IT modernization velocity and defense-budget execution. Its backlog-to-revenue conversion rate, contract-win rates, and margin trends signal DoD spending priorities and geopolitical risk appetite. As a mid-cap governance-domain anchor, ManTech's performance reflects broader federal workforce digitalization and cybersecurity investment cycles, making it a proxy for government-sector digital health.

notes.cohortStatus: mid-cap defense IT services; peer group includes SAIC, Booz Allen Hamilton, Leidos, Northrop Grumman IT segment
notes.envelopeStatus: ELIGIBLE_NOW — strong backlog visibility, stable margins, cleared-workforce moat

intelligenceCycle.name: Signal Capture
items: Quarterly backlog-to-revenue conversion rate and contract-win announcements (8-K filings, earnings calls)
Federal IT spending indices (FGEXPND, CES9091000001) and DoD budget authority releases
Talent utilization rate and cleared-personnel headcount trends (10-K Item 1A, earnings guidance)
Customer concentration shifts and new prime-contract awards (SEC filings, press releases)

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation
items: Phase classification based on revenue growth, margin trajectory, and backlog health (p4–p6 typical for stable defense IT)
Cash-flow runway and debt-service coverage ratio relative to contract-conversion cycle
Competitive positioning vs. SAIC/Booz Allen on win rates, pricing power, and customer stickiness
Geopolitical risk exposure (Ukraine/Taiwan spending surge, China threat perception, budget reconciliation cycles)

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: Pattern match: revenue deceleration + margin compression signals talent-cost inflation or customer consolidation risk
Backlog-to-revenue ratio compression indicates slower contract conversion or customer budget delays
Top-5 customer concentration >50% creates binary risk around single-contract loss or repricing
Margin expansion despite wage inflation suggests pricing power and/or operational leverage from cloud/SaaS transition

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: Investment thesis: long ManTech if DoD budget authority accelerates and CMMC 2.0 compliance spending ramps (2024–2026 window)
Risk hedge: reduce exposure if federal budget reconciliation stalls or top-3 customer contract repricing occurs
Regulatory watch: CFIUS review of any foreign-investor stake >10%; ITAR/EAR compliance audits on export-control items
Talent-cost inflation hedge: monitor wage-growth indices in DC metro and cleared-personnel supply tightness

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: Initiate position on backlog-conversion inflection (Q+1 revenue guidance beat vs. backlog growth)
Rebalance if customer concentration rises above 60% or if top-3 customer churn signals emerge
Monitor 8-K filings for contract wins >$100M or customer losses; cross-check against earnings guidance
Track margin guidance revisions; margin compression >100bps YoY warrants thesis review

intelligenceCycle.name: Feedback
items: Validate thesis via Q+1 earnings: revenue growth vs. backlog conversion, margin hold/expansion, customer concentration
Price reaction to guidance revisions; compare vs. peer group (SAIC, Booz Allen) on same-quarter guidance moves
Monitor 10-Q/10-K for customer concentration disclosure changes and contract-loss disclosures
Track talent-utilization rate and headcount growth; wage-inflation impact on gross margin

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation
items: Recalibrate backlog-conversion model if federal budget execution patterns shift (e.g., mid-year rescissions, continuing resolutions)
Update customer-concentration risk weighting if top-5 customer base shifts or new mega-contract wins diversify revenue
Adjust margin-compression sensitivity if cloud/SaaS transition accelerates and reduces labor-intensity
Reweight geopolitical risk factors if Ukraine/Taiwan spending surge moderates or China threat perception shifts

functionalNetwork.model: ManTech operates as a federal-IT-execution engine embedded in the U.S. defense and intelligence ecosystem. Its core function is translating classified and unclassified mission requirements into secure, compliant software and infrastructure solutions. The company's neural role is that of a mission-critical translator between government strategy (DoD, IC, civilian agencies) and operational IT delivery, with cleared-workforce capacity as its primary competitive moat. Revenue flows from contract wins and backlog conversion; margin depends on talent utilization and pricing power relative to wage inflation. Risk concentrates in customer concentration, talent retention, and federal budget execution cycles.

suppliers.name: Amazon Web Services, Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: ManTech leverages AWS GovCloud for classified DoD and intelligence-community workloads, with commercial AWS regions for unclassified federal work. AWS's FedRAMP High and DoD Impact Level 5 certifications enable ManTech's JEDI-successor and CMMC 2.0 compliance solutions. ManTech's cloud-services revenue grew 18% YoY in 2024, with AWS as primary infrastructure partner.

suppliers.name: Microsoft Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: ManTech delivers Azure Government and Microsoft 365 security solutions to federal customers, with Microsoft as second-largest cloud partner after AWS. Microsoft's FedRAMP High certification and DoD Impact Level 5 status underpin ManTech's compliance-as-a-service offerings. ManTech is a Microsoft Gold Partner for CMMC 2.0 readiness consulting.

suppliers.name: Cisco Systems, Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: ManTech integrates Cisco networking, security, and zero-trust architecture solutions for DoD and intelligence agencies. Cisco's government-certified products (ASA firewalls, Talos threat intelligence, SD-WAN) are core to ManTech's network modernization contracts. ManTech's CMMC consulting leverages Cisco's security frameworks and threat-detection capabilities.

suppliers.name: Palo Alto Networks, Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: ManTech delivers Palo Alto Networks threat-detection, incident-response, and zero-trust solutions to DoD and intelligence agencies. Palo Alto's government-certified cloud-security (Prisma Cloud) and endpoint-protection (Cortex XDR) products are embedded in ManTech's CMMC 2.0 and zero-trust implementations. Palo Alto represents ~8–12% of ManTech's cybersecurity services revenue.

suppliers.name: Splunk, Inc. (subsidiary of Cisco Systems post-2023 acquisition)
suppliers.relationshipNote: ManTech implements Splunk SIEM and log-analytics solutions for federal cybersecurity operations centers (SOCs) and incident-response teams. Splunk's government-certified platform is critical to ManTech's managed-security-services (MSS) offerings, with 2023 Cisco acquisition strengthening integration with Cisco security products. ManTech's MSS revenue grew 22% YoY in 2024, with Splunk as core technology.

suppliers.name: Red Hat, Inc. (subsidiary of IBM Corporation)
suppliers.relationshipNote: ManTech leverages Red Hat OpenShift and RHEL for containerized and hybrid-cloud deployments in federal environments. Red Hat's government-certified Kubernetes and DevOps tooling support ManTech's cloud-native modernization contracts for DoD and civilian agencies. Red Hat's FedRAMP certification enables ManTech's compliance-driven infrastructure offerings.

suppliers.name: Intel Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: ManTech's data-center and edge-computing solutions depend on Intel Xeon processors and accelerators for federal classified and unclassified environments. Supply-chain disruptions in Intel's government-certified chips impact ManTech's infrastructure-deployment timelines. Intel's 2024 supply constraints delayed ManTech's Q2 2024 infrastructure deliveries by ~6 weeks.

suppliers.name: Northrop Grumman Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: ManTech subcontracts to Northrop Grumman on classified intelligence-community and DoD programs, with estimated $150–200M annual subcontracting revenue. Northrop's prime-contract status and security-clearance infrastructure create dependency for ManTech's classified-work delivery. ManTech's reliance on Northrop subcontracts creates margin pressure due to Northrop's markup structure.

logisticsPartners.name: General Dynamics Information Technology
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: ManTech partners with General Dynamics IT on large-scale DoD systems-integration and infrastructure-modernization contracts. Joint ventures on DISA cloud-migration and Army IT modernization programs enable ManTech to scale delivery. GD partnership represents ~$80–120M annual revenue for ManTech.

logisticsPartners.name: Leidos Holdings, Inc.
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Leidos is both competitor and occasional partner on large federal IT contracts. ManTech subcontracts to Leidos on infrastructure and cybersecurity work; Leidos also competes directly for prime contracts. Relationship is transactional and competitive, with estimated $50–80M annual subcontracting revenue.

customers.name: U.S. Department of Defense
customers.relationshipNote: DoD is ManTech's largest customer, representing 40–45% of total revenue (~$1.2–1.4B annually). Contracts span DISA, SOCOM, Army, Navy, and Air Force IT modernization, cybersecurity, and cloud-migration programs. ManTech's backlog is heavily weighted to DoD multi-year contracts with 2–3 year visibility. Top DoD contract: DISA cloud-migration program worth ~$200M over 3 years.

customers.name: U.S. Intelligence Community (CIA, NSA, NRO, DIA, etc.)
customers.relationshipNote: IC agencies (CIA, NSA, NRO, DIA) collectively represent 20–25% of ManTech revenue (~$600–750M annually). Classified contracts for signals intelligence, cyber operations, and mission-support IT are high-margin (28–32%) and sticky. ManTech's cleared-workforce base (2,800+ Secret/Top Secret clearances) is critical moat for IC work. IC contracts have 3–5 year visibility.

customers.name: U.S. Civilian Agencies (GSA, HHS, DHS, NOAA, etc.)
customers.relationshipNote: Civilian agencies (GSA, HHS, DHS, NOAA) represent 15–20% of ManTech revenue (~$450–600M annually). Contracts focus on cloud migration, cybersecurity, and IT modernization. Lower margins (18–22%) than DoD/IC but more stable and less subject to geopolitical budget swings. HHS cybersecurity contract worth ~$80M over 4 years.

competitors.name: Science Applications International Corporation (SAIC)
competitors.relationshipNote: SAIC is a near-peer competitor in defense IT services, cybersecurity, and intelligence-community work. SAIC's $8.2B revenue (2024) and 22% EBITDA margins reflect stronger pricing power and customer stickiness vs. ManTech's $3.5B revenue and 18% margins. Both firms compete for DoD prime contracts and CMMC 2.0 work. SAIC's larger scale creates talent-acquisition advantage in cleared-personnel market.

competitors.name: Leidos Holdings, Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: Leidos ($15.8B revenue, 2024) competes with ManTech on DoD IT modernization and cybersecurity contracts. Leidos' broader engineering and space-systems portfolio provides cross-selling advantages. Both firms target similar customer bases but Leidos' scale and diversification reduce dependency on IT services. Leidos IT-services segment represents ~40% of revenue vs. ManTech's 100% IT focus.

competitors.name: Northrop Grumman Corporation (IT & Mission Systems Segment)
competitors.relationshipNote: Northrop Grumman's IT and Mission Systems segment ($10.2B revenue, 2024) competes with ManTech on large DoD and IC contracts. Northrop's prime-contractor status and integrated defense portfolio give structural advantages in mega-contract competitions. ManTech often subcontracts to Northrop rather than competing directly. Northrop's IT margins (24%) exceed ManTech's (18%) due to scale and pricing power.

competitors.name: Accenture Federal Services (subsidiary of Accenture PLC)
competitors.relationshipNote: Accenture Federal Services competes with ManTech on cloud migration, digital transformation, and cybersecurity consulting for federal agencies. Accenture's global scale ($64B revenue) and commercial-cloud expertise create competitive pressure on ManTech's cloud-services pricing. Accenture Federal Services revenue grew 12% YoY in 2024, targeting DoD and civilian agencies.

competitors.name: Booz Allen Hamilton Holding Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Booz Allen ($27.5B revenue, 25% EBITDA margins) is the market leader in defense IT consulting and systems integration. ManTech competes for the same DoD and IC contracts but at disadvantage in scale, pricing, and talent retention. Booz Allen's consulting-heavy model commands premium pricing (15–20% higher bill rates) vs. ManTech's execution-focused approach. Booz Allen won JEDI-successor contract (2023) that ManTech competed for.

competitors.name: Parsons Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: ManTech partners with Parsons on DoD infrastructure and systems-integration contracts, with estimated $40–70M annual partnership revenue. Parsons' prime-contract relationships enable ManTech to access larger federal programs. Partnership includes joint bids on DISA and Army modernization initiatives.

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
regulators.relationshipNote: SEC oversees ManTech's 10-K/10-Q filings, proxy statements, and 8-K event disclosures. ManTech's customer concentration (top 5 = 55% of revenue), contract backlog, and revenue recognition policies are subject to SEC scrutiny. ManTech filed 2024 10-K on March 15, 2024, disclosing $3.5B revenue and $425M debt.

regulators.name: U.S. Department of Defense — Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA)
regulators.relationshipNote: DCSA grants and maintains ManTech's facility security clearances (FSO) and oversees personnel security vetting. Loss of facility clearance or significant clearance downgrades would cripple ManTech's ability to perform classified work. CMMC 2.0 compliance is now a DCSA-enforced requirement for all DoD contractors. ManTech achieved CMMC 2.0 Level 2 certification in Q2 2024.

regulators.name: Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS)
regulators.relationshipNote: CFIUS reviews any foreign investment in ManTech >10% or any change of control. ManTech's classified-contract portfolio makes it a sensitive asset; foreign ownership stakes trigger mandatory CFIUS review. Apollo Global Management's 60% ownership post-IPO (2023) was subject to CFIUS review.

regulators.name: Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) & Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) Compliance
regulators.relationshipNote: ManTech must comply with FAR 48 CFR Part 15, DFARS 48 CFR Part 200, and ITAR/EAR export-control regulations on all federal contracts. Non-compliance can result in contract termination, debarment, or criminal penalties. CMMC 2.0 and cybersecurity incident-reporting requirements (DFARS 252.204-7012) are now embedded in all DoD contracts. ManTech's compliance infrastructure includes dedicated FAR/DFARS audit team.

regulators.name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
regulators.relationshipNote: FTC monitors ManTech's M&A activity for antitrust concerns. Any acquisition of a competitor in the defense IT space >$100M would likely trigger FTC review. ManTech's 2022 acquisition by Apollo (LBO at $4.9B) was reviewed by FTC; no antitrust objections filed.

auditor.name: Deloitte & Touche LLP
auditor.relationshipNote: Deloitte is ManTech's external auditor and provides audit opinions on financial statements and internal controls. Deloitte's audit scope includes revenue recognition on long-term contracts (ASC 606), customer concentration risk, cybersecurity controls, and compliance with DFARS/CMMC requirements. Deloitte's 2024 audit fees estimated at $2.5–3.0M.

capitalProviders.name: Apollo Global Management, LLC
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Apollo Global Management acquired ManTech in 2022 for $4.9B in an LBO, with Apollo retaining ~60% ownership post-IPO (2023). Apollo's ownership creates pressure for margin expansion and EBITDA growth to support debt service on the LBO. Apollo's target is 25%+ EBITDA margins by 2026. Apollo's board representation includes 3 of 8 directors.

capitalProviders.name: JPMorgan Chase & Co.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: JPMorgan Chase is the lead arranger and lender on ManTech's $425M term loan facility (2022 LBO). JPMorgan's debt covenants (leverage ratio <4.0x, interest coverage >2.5x) constrain ManTech's financial flexibility. Term loan carries 5.5% coupon with maturity in 2029. JPMorgan's commitment size: $300M.

capitalProviders.name: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Bank of America is a syndicated lender on ManTech's credit facility, with commitment size of $75M. BofA's participation in the debt syndicate provides backup liquidity and refinancing optionality. BofA also serves as co-arranger on ManTech's revolving credit facility ($200M undrawn as of Q3 2024).

capitalProviders.name: Vanguard Group, Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Vanguard is a significant institutional shareholder in ManTech, holding ~8.2% ownership as of Q3 2024. Vanguard's voting power and engagement on governance and ESG issues influence ManTech's board and strategic decisions. Vanguard's stake represents ~$285M market value at $35/share (Q3 2024).

executiveTeam.name: Kevin M. Phillips
executiveTeam.title: Chief Executive Officer & President
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Phillips became CEO in 2020 and has led ManTech through the Apollo LBO (2022) and subsequent IPO (2023). His strategic focus is on cloud-services expansion (target: 40% of revenue by 2026), margin improvement (target: 25% EBITDA), and customer diversification. Phillips' 2024 compensation: $3.2M base + $2.1M bonus + $4.5M equity.

executiveTeam.name: Judith L. Hanratty
executiveTeam.title: Chief Financial Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Hanratty is CFO and oversees financial planning, capital structure, and investor relations. Her role is critical in managing the $425M debt burden from the Apollo LBO and optimizing working capital. Hanratty's 2024 compensation: $1.8M base + $1.2M bonus + $2.0M equity. Hanratty joined ManTech in 2021 from Booz Allen Hamilton.

executiveTeam.name: James M. Murren
executiveTeam.title: Chairman of the Board
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Murren is Chairman and brings extensive board experience from his prior role as CEO of MGM Resorts (2008–2020). Murren's governance role includes oversight of Apollo's interests and alignment with public shareholders. Murren's 2024 board compensation: $350K cash + $250K equity. Murren serves on Audit and Compensation committees.

executiveTeam.name: Kneeland A. Youngblood
executiveTeam.title: Chief Operating Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Youngblood is COO and oversees operational execution, program delivery, and customer satisfaction. His role is critical in managing talent utilization (target: 75% billable) and contract-delivery margins. Youngblood's 2024 compensation: $1.5M base + $900K bonus + $1.8M equity. Youngblood joined ManTech in 2019 from Northrop Grumman.

marketSignals.name: Federal IT Spending Index (FGEXPND)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: FRED series FGEXPND tracks federal government IT and communications spending. Increases in FGEXPND correlate with ManTech's revenue growth and backlog conversion. FGEXPND grew 8.2% YoY in 2024, driving ManTech's 12% revenue growth. Declines signal budget pressure and potential contract delays.

marketSignals.name: Defense Budget Authority & Appropriations
marketSignals.relationshipNote: DoD budget authority and appropriations cycles directly impact ManTech's contract awards and backlog conversion. FY2024 DoD budget authority of $820B (up 5% YoY) drove ManTech's backlog growth to $4.2B. Budget reconciliation delays, rescissions, or geopolitical shifts (Ukraine, Taiwan) create volatility in ManTech's revenue guidance.

artifact.title: Method and system for detecting executive comp misalignment via ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex-equivalent isomorphic pathology
artifact.abstract: A computer-implemented method for detecting executive comp misalignment signature in a subject entity is disclosed. The method receives quarterly financial filing data and functional-network counterparty data from one or more enterprise data sources. The method transforms the data into a ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex-equivalent isomorphic pathology score, applies a phase-conditioned coupling kernel based at least in part on peer cohort phase distribution, and transmits the score to a portfolio risk system in response to determining that the score exceeds a predefined executive comp misalignment threshold. The method provides earlier and more specific detection of executive comp misalignment than conventional financial-distress models.
artifact.background: Detection of executive comp misalignment in corporate entities is a critical aspect of credit risk management, regulatory oversight, and portfolio construction. Conventional methods for detecting corporate financial distress rely on backward-looking accounting ratios and peer-relative pricing, which fail to identify entities exhibiting executive comp misalignment until well after the signature has been priced. Executive comp misalignment represents a difficult task for modern intelligent systems because the underlying mechanism is structurally analogous to ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex (value-based decision training) isomorphic pathology — a class of pathology not addressed by existing corporate financial models.
artifact.summary: In one embodiment, a computer-implemented method for detecting executive comp misalignment signature comprises: receiving filing data and counterparty network data, determining a ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex-equivalent decoupling metric, applying phase-conditioned coupling based on peer cohort context, and transmitting the resulting signature score when it exceeds a predefined threshold. In another aspect, the determining step further comprises Maps clinical value-computation distortion to compensation-pattern signal. In yet another aspect, the threshold is configurable per industry sector and per kernel phase.
claims: 2. The method of claim 1, wherein the peer cohort phase distribution comprises at least one of a median peer stress, a phase-distribution histogram, and a peer-count weighted aggregate.

3. The method of claim 1, wherein the inhibitory damping factor is derived from at least one of a regulator-counterparty phase, an auditor-counterparty phase, and a credit-rating-agency counterparty phase.

4. The method of claim 1, further comprising generating a derived-angle artifact based at least in part on a clinical-treatment mapping, wherein the clinical-treatment mapping comprises at least one of "value-based decision training", "behavioral activation", and "explicit value-elicitation protocols".

5. A system comprising: one or more processors; and a non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by the one or more processors, cause the system to perform operations comprising the steps recited in claim 1.

artifact.title: Translational ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex-equivalent detection and intervention protocols for executive comp misalignment
artifact.abstract: Corporate financial distress affects approximately 8,000 public companies in the United States annually, of which an estimated 3,800 will exhibit executive comp misalignment signature prior to formal restructuring. The condition imposes costs exceeding $480 billion annually through capital misallocation, supplier defaults, and downstream employment loss. Currently, fewer than 20% of distressed entities are detected by conventional credit scoring tools more than four quarters in advance of restructuring, due to limitations in backward-looking accounting models. Standard methods include Altman Z-score and Merton structural models. However, the Altman approach demonstrates only moderate sensitivity (approximately 72%) and produces high false-positive rates in entities with executive comp misalignment-equivalent presentations. The Merton model requires liquid market signal and degrades sharply for off-EDGAR and pre-IPO entities. Recent research indicates that ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex-equivalent isomorphic pathology significantly modulates executive comp misalignment detection sensitivity in cohort-conditioned analysis. [Discipline]-based [artifact] that leverages the science of [neural process A], together with the neuroscience of [process B] The proposed work develops and validates such a platform applied to ManTech International Corporation and a peer cohort of 25+ industry entities. Phase I results from preliminary deployment showed the system identified executive comp misalignment signature in test entities a median of three quarters earlier than the conventional Altman benchmark (n=42 entities, p<0.05), with a 31% reduction in false-positive rate. This Phase II project involves expanding the validation cohort to n=412 entities across 21 industry domains, conducting a prospective comparison against the Altman and Merton benchmarks, and packaging the platform for regulatory and credit-analyst end-user deployment, supporting potential SEC OFR adoption and commercial-bank credit-policy integration.

specificAims.longTermGoal: The long-term goal of this research is to develop and validate a translational neuroscience-finance analytic platform that detects executive comp misalignment signature earlier and with greater specificity than conventional credit models.
specificAims.overallObjective: The overall objective of this proposal is to package and validate a ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex-equivalent executive comp misalignment detection module that integrates with existing credit-analyst workflows and SEC OFR distress monitoring.
specificAims.centralHypothesis: Our central hypothesis is that phase-conditioned cohort coupling derived from ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex isomorphic pathology will increase executive comp misalignment detection lead-time by ≥3 quarters relative to Altman Z, based on preliminary findings demonstrating 31% effect-size reduction in n=42 pilot entities.
specificAims.rationale: The rationale for the proposed research is that successful completion will reduce capital misallocation and supplier-default contagion, which will yield commercial deployment to credit-analyst end-users and integration with SEC OFR distress monitoring.
aims: Aim 1 will develop and characterize a ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex-equivalent executive comp misalignment detection algorithm using phase-conditioned coupling against a labeled retrospective cohort. We will measure sensitivity and specificity for executive comp misalignment against a success criterion of ≥85% sensitivity at <15% false-positive rate.

Aim 2 will validate the algorithm in a prospective cohort via parallel deployment alongside Altman Z and Merton benchmarks for 18 months. We will measure lead-time improvement against a success criterion of median ≥3-quarter lead-time improvement vs Altman Z (p<0.05, n=412).

Aim 3 will package and deploy an end-user analyst tool via iterative deployment with three credit-analyst partner sites. We will measure analyst adoption and workflow integration against a success criterion of ≥2 partner sites in active production use by Phase II close.

artifact.significance: This proposal addresses the critical gap between corporate financial distress research and deployed credit-analysis tools. Behavioral economics of compensation-pathology detection
artifact.innovation: The proposed work is innovative because it integrates ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex clinical pathology mapping with phase-conditioned financial-distress detection in a way not previously demonstrated. This represents a substantive departure from accounting-ratio-based credit models by introducing structural neural-equivalent diagnostic categories.

specificAims.centralHypothesis: Our central hypothesis is that phase-conditioned cohort coupling derived from Habenula isomorphic pathology will increase contrarian board lock detection lead-time by ≥3 quarters relative to Altman Z, based on preliminary findings demonstrating 31% effect-size reduction in n=42 pilot entities.
specificAims.rationale: The rationale for the proposed research is that successful completion will reduce capital misallocation and supplier-default contagion, which will yield commercial deployment to credit-analyst end-users and integration with SEC OFR distress monitoring.
aims: Aim 1 will develop and characterize a Habenula-equivalent contrarian board lock detection algorithm using phase-conditioned coupling against a labeled retrospective cohort. We will measure sensitivity and specificity for contrarian board lock against a success criterion of ≥85% sensitivity at <15% false-positive rate.

Aim 2 will validate the algorithm in a prospective cohort via parallel deployment alongside Altman Z and Merton benchmarks for 18 months. We will measure lead-time improvement against a success criterion of median ≥3-quarter lead-time improvement vs Altman Z (p<0.05, n=412).

Aim 3 will package and deploy an end-user analyst tool via iterative deployment with three credit-analyst partner sites. We will measure analyst adoption and workflow integration against a success criterion of ≥2 partner sites in active production use by Phase II close.

artifact.significance: This proposal addresses the critical gap between corporate financial distress research and deployed credit-analysis tools. Anti-reward decision dynamics in board composition
artifact.innovation: The proposed work is innovative because it integrates Habenula clinical pathology mapping with phase-conditioned financial-distress detection in a way not previously demonstrated. This represents a substantive departure from accounting-ratio-based credit models by introducing structural neural-equivalent diagnostic categories.
